nodes.name: Building and drawing shapes
nodes.description: Represent shapes seen in everyday objects by making models from simple parts and by drawing their shapes.
criteria: Choose a familiar object and identify the shape to represent.
Build recognizable plane and solid shape models using parts such as sticks, clay or connectors.
Draw a recognizable shape from an everyday object and explain how the drawing or model matches it.

nodes.name: Identifying measurable attributes
nodes.description: Identify properties of an object that can be measured, distinguishing such attributes as length, height, weight and capacity.
criteria: Name the attribute described by a measurement question, such as how long, how heavy or how much a container holds.
Describe more than one measurable attribute of the same object.
Clarify which attribute is meant when an object is described as big or small.

nodes.name: Measuring length with repeated equal units
nodes.description: Measure an object whose length is a whole number of chosen units by lining up equal copies of a shorter length and counting how many span the object.
criteria: Place equal length units from one endpoint to the other with adjacent ends touching.
Count the units and report both the number and the chosen unit.
Explain or correct a measurement that uses gaps, overlaps or unequal units.

nodes.name: Reading clocks to the hour and half hour
nodes.description: Read and write whole-hour and half-hour times, connecting analog hand positions with digital notation.
criteria: Read an analog clock at a whole hour or half hour and write the corresponding digital time.
Read a digital time ending in :00 or :30 and show it on an analog clock.
Place the hour hand between successive hour numbers at half past and explain which hour has begun.

nodes.name: Connecting counting with addition and subtraction
nodes.description: Use forward or backward counting to represent addition and subtraction within 20, keeping track of how many one-unit changes are made.
criteria: Start from a given addend and count forward by the other addend to find a sum within 20.
Count backward from a starting number to subtract a small whole number, or count up to find the difference.
Explain how the counted steps correspond to the number added or subtracted, rather than counting the starting number as a step.

nodes.name: Equality and true or false number sentences
nodes.description: Interpret the equal sign as a claim that the expressions on its two sides have the same value, and check addition and subtraction number sentences within 20.
criteria: Explain that an equality compares two values, including when an operation is written on the right.
Decide whether an addition or subtraction number sentence is true or false by comparing its two sides.
Recognize equal values in different forms, including expressions on both sides, and justify the decision with numbers or objects.

nodes.name: Partitioning rectangles into square grids
nodes.description: Divide a rectangle into complete rows and columns of equal squares and count the squares in the resulting array.
criteria: Draw or construct a grid that fills a rectangle with equal squares in aligned rows and columns.
Identify the number of rows and the number of squares in each row.
Count all the squares without omissions or double counting and explain how the row or column structure helps.

nodes.name: How length measurements depend on unit size
nodes.description: Measure the same length with two differently sized units and explain why a smaller unit produces a larger numerical measurement.
criteria: Measure one object twice, using a consistent unit size within each measurement and a different unit size for the second.
Report each result with its unit and compare the two numerical measurements.
Explain that the object keeps the same length while more smaller units or fewer larger units are needed to span it.

nodes.name: Reading clocks in five-minute intervals
nodes.description: Read and write times shown in five-minute increments on analog and digital clocks, and use a.m. or p.m. to locate the time within a day.
criteria: Read an analog clock with its minute hand on a five-minute mark and write the matching digital time; read a digital time whose minutes are a multiple of five.
Show a given five-minute time with both hands in appropriate positions, including an hour hand between hour numbers.
Choose a.m. or p.m. for a time in a daily-event context and explain the distinction around midday and midnight.

nodes.name: Word problems with US dollars and cents
nodes.description: Find totals, purchases and change involving US dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies. Calculate in whole dollars or whole cents and express the result in the chosen unit.
criteria: Use the values of US pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters and dollar bills to find the total value of a collection in whole cents or, when applicable, whole dollars.
Represent and solve a purchase, combined-value or change story using whole-number addition or subtraction in a single currency unit and explain the answer in context.
Use 100 cents per dollar when expressing amounts in a common unit, and label a whole-dollar result with the dollar symbol or a whole-cent result with the cent symbol.

nodes.name: Measuring area with unit squares
nodes.description: Measure a plane region by covering it with equal unit squares without gaps or overlaps. Interpret the count as area in square units, using standard or chosen square units.
criteria: Cover a region that can be tiled by whole unit squares, checking that the squares fill it without gaps or overlaps.
Count the squares and explain why that count gives the region's area in the chosen square unit.
Measure or interpret tiled regions using square centimeters, square meters, square inches, square feet and improvised square units.
Reject a square count as an area measurement when square sizes are mixed or the covering has gaps or overlaps.

edges.scope: Models and drawings of familiar rectangles, squares, triangles and circles
edges.rationale: Recognizing a familiar plane shape provides a target for choosing parts and checking the drawing. The Geometry Progression explicitly connects familiar shape images and names with informal representation. This does not claim that naming all shapes is necessary before any building activity.

edges.scope: Recognizing familiar cubes, cuboids, cylinders and spheres when choosing or checking a solid model
edges.rationale: The existing node identifies these solid shapes in real objects. Recognizing a target's shape helps a learner choose parts and check a model against it. The Geometry Progression connects familiar solid-shape images with construction activities; this is useful preparation for the solid-model portion, not a requirement to name every solid before building.

edges.scope: Choosing length as the attribute measured by an end-to-end chain of units
edges.rationale: Distinguishing length from other ways an object can be big helps the learner decide what the chain of units measures. The Geometric Measurement Progression separates identifying an attribute from assigning it a numerical measure.

edges.scope: Extending analog/digital correspondence from :00 and :30 to other multiples of five minutes
edges.rationale: The same hour and minute hands and digital hour/minute fields are used at both precisions. Familiar whole-hour and half-hour cases provide reference positions for locating the intermediate five-minute times; this is useful preparation, not a claim that one teaching order is compulsory.

edges.scope: Following successive number names when crossing from smaller sums to ten
edges.rationale: The existing node assesses the sequence from six to ten and the successor of nine. That sequence is a concrete part of counting forward across these values, although it does not by itself cover the full within-20 counting procedure.

edges.scope: Moving from equal quantities within five to equal-valued expressions
edges.rationale: The existing node explicitly interprets equal as the same amount. That idea supports comparing the values represented on both sides of an equation; it does not supply the expression or equation-truth tasks. IM's Equality Number Sentences uses equal object collections to support this move.

edges.scope: Composing a rectangle from square pieces before constructing its complete row-and-column partition
edges.rationale: The existing node assembles familiar figures from simple plane shapes, including squares, and counts the pieces. The Geometry Progression identifies shape composition as preparation for spatial structuring. A complete array adds equal-size squares, aligned rows and columns, and full coverage of the rectangle.

edges.scope: Comparing numerical results obtained by correctly measuring one object with two unit sizes
edges.rationale: Laying equal units along the same length makes the inverse relation between unit size and count visible. Students can also compare readings on two differently graduated rulers.

edges.scope: Adding whole-cent amounts in two-digit total-cost or coin-value problems
edges.rationale: Once coin values are represented in cents, a two-digit addition method can combine the amounts. This supports the numerical step but does not teach denomination values, currency notation or interpreting the story, and a written algorithm is not required.

edges.scope: Seeing a rectangular region as a complete array of equal area units
edges.rationale: Partitioning a rectangle creates the equal squares that can later be interpreted and counted as area units. IM's Partitioning a Rectangle into Unit Squares and the Geometry Progression explicitly connect this spatial structuring with area measurement. The area node also covers nonrectangular regions, so the relationship is preparation rather than a universal necessity.

edges.scope: Identifying area as region size and using a common area unit before interpreting a square covering
edges.rationale: The existing node identifies area as the size of a surface or closed region and states that comparisons use the same area unit. This helps explain why a covering must use equal-size square units. The Geometric Measurement Progression connects the area attribute, choice of unit and square covering; carrying out and interpreting the covering remain the new node's performances.

edges.scope: Understanding a ruler's centimeter intervals as repeated equal lengths
edges.rationale: The new node gives meaning to the count of equal length intervals that a centimeter ruler records. The existing node assesses using a ruler for whole centimeters but does not explicitly assess constructing the chain of equal units.

edges.scope: Understanding rectangle and square area formulas as counts of square units
edges.rationale: The tiled-region interpretation explains what length times width counts. The Geometric Measurement Progression develops that interpretation before treating multiplication as a formula; knowing the formula alone does not certify the tiling procedure.

reviews.coverageReason: The new node assesses both building shape models from components and drawing shapes from everyday objects. Existing shape naming and combining ready-made plane shapes provide preparation but omit those performances.

sources.note: K.G.B.5 explicitly includes modeling real-world shapes by building from parts and drawing. The legacy task collection has no task for this standard.
Saved Marble topic mt_2VR963szuk, Building & Drawing Shapes, supplies triangle-building, rectangle-drawing and cube-model evidence. Its dependency lists were not imported.
Geometry, Kindergarten, printed pp.117-118 connects familiar plane and solid shape images and names to construction activities, informal drawings and models made from components.

alignments.reason: Both required representations are explicit criteria, including representing shapes encountered in the world.

reviews.coverageReason: The new node explicitly identifies several measurable attributes of one object. Centimeter, mass-unit and capacity nodes assume particular attributes and do not assess selecting or distinguishing several attributes.

sources.note: K.MD.A.1 requires describing measurable attributes and several attributes of one object, without requiring numerical measurement.

Saved topic mt_NtJYlJdUe9 assesses multiple attributes of one bottle. Related mt_uhuxX8sg9f, mt_-P1kdZhHbL and mt_zkFbMLpu3U focus on comparing particular attributes and do not alone establish the multiple-attribute scope.
Geometric Measurement, Kindergarten, printed pp.6-7 distinguishes length, area, volume and weight when children use undifferentiated big/small language.

alignments.reason: Naming the relevant attribute and describing multiple measurable properties of a single object cover the complete requested performance.

reviews.coverageReason: The new repeated-unit node assesses the physical measuring procedure and its meaning, restricted to whole-unit spans. A ruler measurement in centimeters does not establish correct placement of repeated units.

sources.note: 1.MD.A.2 specifies same-size units, a complete end-to-end span without gaps or overlaps, and whole-number lengths.
Saved topic mt_cqSf213hSa assesses measuring with repeated paper clips, interpreting the count, and avoiding gaps or overlaps.
Geometric Measurement, Grade 1, printed pp.8-10 describes counting equal physical units and common placement errors; it distinguishes measurement from comparison alone.

alignments.reason: The new procedure retains unit equality, endpoint coverage, unit counting and the whole-unit restriction.

reviews.coverageReason: The new hour/half-hour node directly assesses reading and writing both clock representations. Time-unit conversion, elapsed-time calculation and 24-hour notation do not certify reading analog hand positions.

sources.note: 1.MD.B.3 specifies hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks; the legacy IM collection supplies the standard but no task.
Saved topic mt_0XxyaQLRhn includes analog/digital matching and placing the hour hand between hour numbers for half past.

IM Ordering Time extends the same two representations through increasingly fine time-card sets. This supports a preparation connection to five-minute reading, without treating curriculum order as a necessary prerequisite.

alignments.reason: Both clock types and both specified time increments are assessed explicitly.

reviews.coverageReason: The new node assesses the connection between count steps and the arithmetic operation. Existing addition, subtraction and make-ten nodes assess answers or different strategies and do not certify counting on or back.

sources.note: 1.OA.C.5 requires relating counting to addition and subtraction, with counting on as an example.
Saved topic mt_PpWSHA-0kv includes starting at an addend, counting on, counting back for subtraction, and explaining the arithmetic connection.

IM The Very Hungry Caterpillar connects added counters to equations and explicitly discusses counting-on development. Its instructional totals can exceed 20, while the new assessment scope stays within 20.
Operations and Algebraic Thinking, Grade 1, explains the move from counting all to Level 2 counting methods and relates successive counts to arithmetic changes.

alignments.reason: Criteria require executing and explaining the counting connection for both addition and subtraction in the cluster's range.

reviews.coverageReason: The new node makes relational equality and equation truth explicit. The existing quantity-comparison node covers equal amounts only, while equality-property and equation-solving nodes concern transformations or unknowns rather than the full early number-sentence task.

sources.note: 1.OA.D.7 includes equations with an operation on the right or on both sides, and both true and false claims.
Saved topic mt_oIzycTBeE4 distinguishes equal value from an instruction to produce an answer and includes deciding a false addition equation.
IM Equality Number Sentences connects equally sized collections to different expressions on the two sides; merely giving the total is insufficient.
Introduction, printed p.3 discusses relational equality and the obstacle caused by interpreting the sign only as an instruction to compute.

alignments.reason: Equal-value meaning, nonstandard equation layouts, and true/false judgments for both operations are explicit.

reviews.coverageReason: The new grid node explicitly assesses making the square partition and counting it. Shape composition, repeated-addition meaning and rectangle area formulas alone do not establish the partitioning performance.

sources.note: 2.G.A.2 requires partitioning into equal squares arranged in rows and columns and counting their total; the standard does not yet require area terminology or a multiplication formula.
Saved topic mt_UTnDKQkVX5 requires dividing the rectangle and connecting its square array to counting.
IM Partitioning a Rectangle into Unit Squares has students draw the grid, count and verify squares, and represent row/column totals. Commentary links the construction to later area work.
Geometry, printed pp.115-116 identifies shape composition as preparation for spatial structuring; Grade 2, printed p.122 develops complete rows and columns that support later area concepts.

alignments.reason: The node assesses constructing the specified partition and counting all of its squares without requiring later area or formula knowledge.

reviews.coverageReason: The new unit-size node assesses repeated measurement and its inverse numerical relationship. Existing unit-conversion nodes do not ask the learner to measure the same object twice or explain why the numerical result changes.

sources.note: 2.MD.A.2 requires two measurements of one length with different unit lengths and an explanation connecting result and unit size.
Saved topic mt_jHv4BgRK8B uses measuring one desk in centimeters and inches and explaining the larger count for the smaller unit.
IM Grade 2 Unit 3 Lesson 1, Standard Units of Measure, builds on 1.MD.A.2, uses straws and centimeter cubes, and compares different counts for the same object.
Geometric Measurement, Grade 2, printed p.13 explicitly relates a larger unit to fewer copies spanning a fixed length.

alignments.reason: Both correct measurements and the conceptual comparison are explicit criteria; no numerical conversion algorithm is substituted for them.

reviews.coverageReason: The new five-minute node covers both clock representations and the a.m./p.m. requirement. The separate hour/half-hour node provides an earlier checkpoint; 24-hour notation and elapsed-time calculations do not fill the remaining scope.

sources.note: 2.MD.C.7 specifies nearest-five-minute readings and writings from analog and digital clocks, with a.m. and p.m.

Saved mt_HNOPGJYiRK covers five-minute analog/digital reading and hand placement, while mt_4m8BimI4G5 supplies the daily-event and a.m./p.m. scope. Both were reviewed before authoring one combined clock procedure.

IM Ordering Time interprets the standard through readings in five-minute increments; set 3 uses minutes that are multiples of five. Its cards distinguish a.m./p.m. and cross midday. This supports the node's five-minute-mark tasks without making rounding from arbitrary minute-hand positions mandatory.

alignments.reason: Five-minute readings, both displays, written times and day-half labels are all assessed explicitly.

reviews.coverageReason: The new concept covers the specified US denominations, word problems and dollar or cent notation, with calculations expressed in a single whole-number currency unit. The existing Renminbi concept uses a different set of denominations.

sources.note: 2.MD.C.8 names dollar bills and four coin types, requires word problems and appropriate dollar/cent notation, and includes valuing a mixed-coin collection.
Saved mt_3tz3Otap5j includes coin totals, change stories and notation. Related mt_cPZwlUk8Nd uses UK coin values and cannot substitute for the named US denominations.
Grade 2 Measurement and Data, printed p.20 names the US denominations and dollar/cent symbols and gives a whole-cent coin-total example.
IM Jamir's Penny Jar represents mixed-coin totals by whole-number addition in cents and explicitly encourages the cent symbol, supporting calculations in a single whole-number currency unit.

alignments.reason: Both the standard and the concept assess solving problems using the named US coins and bills and expressing monetary amounts in the appropriate notation.

reviews.coverageReason: The combined square-unit node explicitly connects a valid whole-square covering to its numerical area and also assesses carrying out the measurement. The existing meaning-of-area and formula nodes omit that covering/count interpretation.

sources.note: Grade 3 Measurement and Data, printed p.25, 3.MD.5b defines the area from the number of unit squares in a covering without gaps or overlaps.

Saved mt_6xNmQLzuqm explicitly assesses unit-square meaning and interpreting a 12-square covering. It is useful semantic evidence even though the saved alignment catalogue does not separately link the 5b subcode.
Geometric Measurement, Grade 3, printed pp.16-17 treats choosing area units, covering a region and counting units together before developing area formulas.

alignments.reason: The covering/count interpretation is an explicit criterion, and the same node additionally assesses performing the 3.MD.C.6 measurement with named square units.

reviews.coverageReason: The combined square-unit node assesses measuring by counting standard and improvised unit squares, with the valid-covering meaning retained. Rectangle formulas, area conversions and the general area concept alone do not establish that procedure.

sources.note: 3.MD.C.6 explicitly lists square centimeters, meters, inches, feet and improvised units for measurement by square counting.

Saved mt_y1n0Zwhoca assesses counting squares in an L-shaped region and using square-centimeter tiles. Related mt_Jvvh5P06NV additionally connects rectangle tiling to multiplication; that extra formula claim is not needed for this node.

IM Finding the Area of Polygons uses square-inch grids. Commentary distinguishes basic whole-square counts in parts (a) and (c) from extensions involving rearranged half-squares, which are not made mandatory here.
IM Partitioning a Rectangle into Unit Squares explains why constructing a complete square grid supports later area understanding, supporting the scoped preparation edge.

alignments.reason: All specified unit families and the square-count procedure are covered, together with the conceptual covering interpretation of 3.MD.C.5b; the two closely overlapping standards share one node.
